brief.headline: Database Guardian could not produce a grounded proposal
brief.what_broke: 12 session(s) waiting on locks. Root blocker(s): pid 342413 (batch_worker/batch_replayable_inventory, idle in transaction, txn open 11.2s) blocks 1 session(s); last statement: SELECT 1
brief.who_is_affected: Checkout success 28% over 30s (87/120 failed) vs SLO 95%. Revenue run-rate $18,400/min; about $13,340/min at risk. Verification window 10s. The business tolerates at most 60s of degraded checkout.

options.description: Terminate the root blocker session (batch_worker/batch_replayable_inventory, pid 342413) to release its locks.
Take no action; let the blocker finish and monitor checkout recovery.
options.cost: about $13,340/min of checkout revenue at risk while waiting

brief.recommendation: Waiting would cost ~$197,610 in lost checkout revenue (889s at $13,340/min) and exceeds the 60s degradation tolerance. Terminating the batch_replayable_inventory job costs only a 4-minute replay (policy may_interrupt). However, invariant I2 requires biz.change_calendar evidence before accepting termination. Since waiting is not viable per I7, we must obtain the change calendar to evaluate termination.

audit.report: A replayable batch job (inventory_reconcile, pid 342413) held a transaction open and blocked checkout, degrading success to 28% over 30 seconds with $13,340/min revenue at risk. The Database Guardian proposed waiting, but the Continuity Guardian rejected it because waiting would exceed the 60-second degradation tolerance and cost ~$197,610 in lost revenue versus a 4-minute replay cost. The Continuity Guardian required change-calendar evidence before approving termination; the calendar showed no active window covering the batch job. The Database Guardian then failed to produce a grounded proposal twice, triggering escalation to the inventory-platform team after 85 seconds with no automated action taken.
audit.root_cause: The Database Guardian proposed waiting despite clear evidence that waiting would far exceed the business's 60-second tolerance, then failed to produce a grounded termination proposal after the Continuity Guardian's revision request.
lessons: For inventory_reconcile (batch_replayable_inventory): pre-load change-calendar status into the runbook so the Database Guardian can immediately propose termination with required evidence when checkout is blocked.
For inventory_reconcile: add a guardrail that auto-rejects 'wait' proposals when expected remaining runtime exceeds the business degradation tolerance (here 889s vs 60s).

For inventory_reconcile: ensure the Database Guardian's proposal template includes the termination action with replay cost (4 min) and policy (may_interrupt) so it can respond to a revision request in one round.
audit.negotiation_critique: The Database Guardian wasted round 1 by proposing wait despite BIZ-4 showing waiting would cost ~$197,610 and exceed the 60s tolerance; after the Continuity Guardian's revision request, the Database Guardian missed the available change-calendar evidence (returned in the same round) and failed grounding twice, forcing escalation.
follow_ups: Update the inventory_reconcile runbook with change-calendar check and termination-first guidance for checkout-blocking scenarios.
Add a policy rule to reject 'wait' when expected blocker runtime > business degradation tolerance.
Verify the Database Guardian's proposal generator includes termination with replay metadata for batch_replayable workloads.

events.title: 3 candidate actions enumerated from observed evidence

candidates.description: Terminate the root blocker session (batch_worker/batch_replayable_inventory, pid 342413) to release its locks.

Hand the decision to the owning team with a decision brief.

proposal.rationale: The blocker (pid 342413) is a batch_replayable_inventory worker idle in transaction for only 4.1s with last statement 'SELECT 1', suggesting it may complete shortly. Checkout is degraded (55% success per TEL-1, 77% per BIZ-1 vs 95% SLO) with $4,155/min at risk, but the business tolerates up to 60s of degradation per BIZ-1. Since the blocker appears to be a short-lived transaction and we lack workload registry data to assess replayability/interrupt policy, waiting briefly to observe if it self-resolves is lower risk than terminating an unknown batch workload.
proposal.expected_effect: If the blocker commits/rolls back within seconds, locks release and checkout recovers without intervention. If it persists beyond ~30s, we'll have more data to decide on terminate or escalate.
proposal.risk_assessment: Checkout continues degrading during wait; if blocker holds locks for >60s total, we breach business tolerance. Terminating blindly could corrupt batch state or violate unknown replay contracts.
